topic.title: Energy prices outran the headline inflation rate: what a household that drives a lot really faces

title: Energy up 20.4% while prices rose 3.7%: what is your real inflation?
description: US prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, but energy rose 20.4%, driven mostly by fuel. Take a home spending $3,000 a year on energy and see why your own inflation can be far above the headline. Speak to a licensed financial adviser in your country before making financial decisions. Illustrative only. Not financial advice.

lines.text: 20.4%. That is how much US energy prices rose in one year.
But the official rate for all prices, in the same report, was just 3.7%.
Then why does filling up my car feel so much worse?
Because the headline is an average basket. Your own rate depends on what you buy.
Say your energy, from fuel to heating and power, costs $3,000 a year.
The headline rate adds $111. The energy average adds $612.
Fuel drove most of that jump. Your energy bill would become $3,612 a year.
If you drive a lot, or heat with oil, your inflation is higher than the news says.
So what is in your basket?

Facts confirmed on the BLS page (https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm, Sept 2026 CPI, released 14 Oct 2026): all items +3.7% (12 mo, NSA), energy +20.4%, core +2.6%, +0.6% m/m SA; all verify items match and the story is current.

Beats 'case' and 'bill', the outro assumption, plan description and title framing apply the 20.4% energy rate to a home's 'gas and power' bills. That is wrong: BLS Table A shows the 20.4% is driven by gasoline (+34.2%) and fuel oil (+74.2%); household energy services rose only 4.6% (electricity +4.4%, utility piped gas +5.0%). A home spending $3,000 a year on gas and power faces about $135-150 more, not $612, and would not pay $3,612. Fix: either make the bill gasoline/fuel (e.g. 'spend $3,000 a year on fuel for your car' at 34.2% or the energy rate clearly labelled as driven by fuel), or use the energy services rate for home bills (would need it added as a sourced fact).

Beat 'rohan' ('why do my bills feel so much worse?', set home, letter prop) and the description ('a home spending $3,000 a year on gas and power') frame utility bills as the item that rose 20.4%; reframe around fuel/gasoline or utilities' actual rate so the conclusion matches the data.
